Alright, so as roguelites go, this one is a little bit short. A lot of stuff is done right, but the flaws really stand out in this game.

Starting with the positive, the production values and the feel of the game are quite well done. The weapons are satisfying to use and the simple art style works very well for the kind of game that is is. At its best, gameplay is frenetic and you are heavily punished even for slight slip ups (and heavily rewarded if you keep on top of positioning the enemies). Also, the game has hats in it.

Now for the rest: first, this is a very easy rogue-lite. I was able to beat the game on my second try, come on. While short, it isn't really all that short: about double the length of the original Binding of Isaac. Nor is it that the game simply is too forgiving. Instead, it ties into the next two problems.

This game lacks variety and randomness that keeps rogue-lites replayable. There are only a few different kinds of enemies and the designs for them (and the bosses) are so basic they might as well have been randomized (they are not). This does mean that once you figure out the mechanics of the game, you can keep yourself alive pretty easily as you are not as much at the mercy of the RNG as in most other rogue-lites (even if you can't find the weapon that you want, it might show up in a vending machine, and in any case, there are not that many and they are not really that different from one another). It doesn't even have that many hats! You're quite likely to see every single hat in the game in a single play-through.

The game rewards spam and standoff fighting far too much. That one reviewer who complained that weapon range is laughably short... well... that is only true of some weapons and not even your starting ones. Many of the weapons have no boundaries to their range, and can easily hit targets off the screen. You can avoid a lot of fighting by just spamming your weapons down unexplored areas and hoping they hit something. This is pretty boring, you have nothing to dodge, and it makes the game easier than it would otherwise be. With the cash magnet, there is no real downside to doing this (and you can confirm your kills without actually checking out where you shot at). If vision range were extended, this would at least feel less cheap and boring.

Finally, there is some minor, but annoying breakage to the game. It doesn't perform well on my Surface Pro 3. Performance does degrade gracefully (the game starts to stretch time, rather than drop frames or stop the world), and this was well done. However it would be nice if this thing could actually run at its full speed most of the time, as gameplay is both more difficult and more exciting when it does. Also, the hat-related achievements currently seem to be broken.

If this game is on sale, go ahead and get it, you'll have enough fun to justify this. However, if you want to play a rogue-lite game, pick up something better and more mainstream, like Enter the Gungeon, Nuclear Throne, or Binding of Isaac: Rebirth.

Good Robot is a lot of fun.  How fun?  Well, the last time I enjoyed a shoot-em-up this much, I was a kid playing Galaga-knockoffs on a monochrome monitor in my father's office.  The game has a lot going for it, including:

- Visuals!  If it moves, kill it.  If it glows, dodge it.  (If it bounces, panic!)  The backgrounds are sparse, but that's a good thing when you're tracking a dozen enemy robots and dodging a screen full of projectiles.

- Sound design!  The game continues to track your bullets after they leave the screen, and you can tell if you've killed something by listening for the tell-tale sound of an exploding robot.  Even better, you can tell whether the the robot dropped cash or loot.  And the music is darned good, too.

- Controls!  You can switch between gamepad and mouse & keyboard on the fly.  Let go of the mouse and pick up the pad--or vice versa--no menus necessary.  You don't even have to pause the game.  (But you probably should.)

- The thrill of discovery!  What do those little icons on the doors mean?  Why not go through and find out?  The game is semi-random, but the patterns are fairly simple.  It's easy to pick up and learn as you go.

I always died with the impression that I could beat that if I were more careful. You know, the kind of difficult people enjoy and take it as a challenge and makes you want to try again. This is the replay mechanism on good robot. You can see this mechanism in effect on strangely unrelated games like Dark Souls and Flappy Birds. I've been waiting for this game for some time, as I'm a great fan of Shamus Young's writing and other exploits on the Spoiler Warning YouTube channel. This game is a twin stick shooter where you play the only "Good Robot" left after a tragic miscalculation by a megacorporation. And you're left to destroy all the robots on a number of environments that seem to have killed all the humans. Your robot has two weapons - a primary rapid firing weapon and a slower heavy hitting weapon and matching primary and secondary is the key to beating a lot of the levels. The robots that you are up against are varied and have different behavior and weapons. You'll often find yourself trying to find a strategy to overcome the combinations of enemies as you can get some very interesting emergent mechanics arising with the different enemies working together. The game has some influences from the old PC game Descent, but as this is a 2D game, it's considerably easier to play. Old 8-bit games such as Robotron and Paradroid on the C-64 as also evident with the visibility of the robots and how your skill in nipping in and out of robots and bullets to avoid trouble. There are elements of a "bullet hell" shooter as well, but as you are more mobile than the bullets and have environmental cover to hide from.  It is extremely survivable as long as you keep moving to use the environment to your advantage.

In addition to the shooting, you can also collect and buy weapons to upgrade your weapons. There also shops for upgrading abilities and also buying "invulnerabity hats" which protect you from attacks. You lose your hat when you are hit. This hat mechanic also adds an additional difficulty level to to the game where you get achievement for keeping your hat. The highest achievement is to keep the same hat to finish the game - which means that you have to avoid being hit in every level. No mean feat, but it does add a considerable challenge for the seasoned gamer. There is also some very good humour text in the menus and news reports reflecting the corporate news media trying to cover up the crisis. Complete with retractions and churnalism.

The graphics are well done with lots of atmosphere for the various level and robot designs. The level scrolls around with parallex layers and fogging and the lighting cone from the robot is a nice touch. The visibility means that you have to keep looking around you to avoid being ambushed from side passages.

The levels are procedurally generated and are different each time to keep the game feeling new. You have a choice of levels to move onto as each are themed - some have certain classes of enemies, some have more money to buy stuff with, some have "special robots" and other have environmental hazards. The final level you choose is the boss level and from there you move onto the next world.  It's nailbiting stuff as you have to juggle your money to replenish your shields and 'lives' whilist buying weapons and performance upgrades. And you can find yourself making life difficult if you can't adapt your playing strategy when a new design of robot turns up.

The music is an electronica soundtrack which changes from world to world. World 3 has a Chinese design and the music has various Asian themes built into it. So there's quite a bit of variety to the music. The sound effects are just what you need for a shooter such as this with audio cues for events you need to watch for such as robots spawing in at the factories and when you find yourself surrounded by heat seeking missiles you need to shoot. 

The overall impression is of an extremely well designed game that draws upon some games from the past to bring them up to date. I've played this for about six hours now and it's proving difficult to put down. There are some some minor issues that the developer is currently patching that don't affect the game, but given that a very small team of put this together and did such a good job, it's well worth the asking price.

It's a pretty solid schmup for a first attempt. The weapons are pretty varied, and offer a deceptive amount of strategy, depending on their power, their cooldown, if any, what enemies you're facing, the level layout, and more. For example, I was rocking in level 3 with a magnetic spiker that dealt big damage(13) every second and pushed the Good Robot back significantly. I decided to switch it out for a pulse laser that dealt 1 damage over time but about 10 times per second - this proved to be likely a mistake as this laser could not destroy missiles, even though it can handle hordes pretty well. 

The music is a calm electronic beat that goes up when a boss fight is present, and changes between levels. The levels are procedurally generated and have small gimmicks, and you can choose which gimmick you want next. 

Also, hats! And humorous blurbs, that give the world a little metaphorical color!

Worth it for the small asking price.
